name: Japanese Black Pine
description: One of the most iconic elements of Japanese gardens. Often trimmed in a bonsai form, these trees are seen as a direct link between the heavens and earth. The needles or 'candles' are trimmed to point upward toward the gods.

name: Flowering Cherry
description: A prominent symbol in Japan, often seen on kimono and confectionery. The cherry symbolizes impermanence — its dormancy is seen as just as beautiful as its blossoms. The wood makes a gray-colored charcoal and the leaves are used to wrap mochi.

name: Wisteria
description: Traditionally used in combination with mulberry trees to make high-quality paper. The fragrant root is used in baths.

name: Azalea
description: Long used as a festival flower. Modern azaleas would not be in such wide production were it not for the work of Japanese gardeners and cultivators.

name: Japanese Camellia
description: Oil pressed from the seeds (tsubaki-abura, 椿油) has been traditionally used in Japan for hair care, and the plant is used to prepare anti-inflammatory medicines. Camellias offer splashes of color and impermanence in the landscape.

name: Sasanqua Camellia
description: A close relative of the Japanese camellia, blooming in autumn and early winter.

name: Japanese Magnolia
description: Bark extract has been used for ~1,000 years in traditional Chinese and Japanese medicine for ailments ranging from asthma to depression to muscle pain.

name: Japanese Maple
description: The leaves are packed around apples and root crops to help preserve them. The wood is used to make instruments and flooring; the leaves are also used in bouquets.

name: Madake Bamboo
description: A large bamboo that sprouts March–April, when its shoots are edible. The leaves are used to wrap rice balls; the wood is used for building and crafting. In the JACCC garden, the bamboo forest represents the future of the Japanese American community — its strength and flexibility.

name: Golden Bamboo
description: An ornamental bamboo cluster forming an evergreen screen.

name: Broad Leaf Bamboo
description: A short, broad-leafed bamboo used widely as understory and groundcover.

name: Camphor
description: The oil of camphor trees is commonly used in industrial applications.

name: Crape Myrtle
description: Known in Japan as Saru Suberi — 'slippery' — from old folklore that the bark is so smooth not even a monkey can climb it.

name: Fortnight Lily
description: Substituted for the lilies of the Man'yōshū to suit the Southern California climate. Traditionally, Japanese lily (Lilium japonicum) and mountain lily (Lilium auratum) would be used.

name: Dwarf Mondo Grass
description: Used in traditional Japanese gardens as a groundcover, especially in geometric settings.

name: Evergreen Pear
description: A substitute for the edible pears commonly found in Japanese gardens. Nashi is the general word for pear.

name: Miniature Japanese Juniper
description: Though not the same juniper found in the Man'yōshū, this dwarf form is widely used as a groundcover in Japanese gardens.

name: Japanese Holly
description: A native plant to Japan. People put a sardine's head with hollies at the entrance of their homes — evils hate the smell of sardines and the jagged leaves of holly. The plant signifies 'defense.'

name: Japanese Pittosporum
description: A native plant to Japan, commonly used in ornamental applications.

name: Japanese Elm
description: A native plant to Japan's forests.

name: Donated Persimmon
description: Donated from Hiroshima — a survivor of the atomic bomb dropped on August 6, 1945. Planted at the JACCC in 2013. Persimmon leaves are traditionally used to wrap food.

name: Baran
description: A broad-leaf plant used in culinary settings — often seen in table settings and used to wrap food.

name: Leather Fern
category_ref_label: Fern (sawarabi 早蕨 / shida 羊歯)
description: Not native to Japan — substituted to suit the Southern California climate. In Japan, ferns are used to help keep food longer.

name: Cedar
description: A towering evergreen used widely in Japanese landscapes and temple architecture. The fragrant wood is prized for construction, sake barrels, and incense.

name: False Heather
description: A low-growing Mexican shrub with tiny lavender flowers, used here as a tidy evergreen groundcover well suited to the Los Angeles climate.

name: Sprenger Asparagus
description: A South African ornamental with arching, feathery foliage. Used as a soft textural groundcover; not native to Japan.

name: Pomegranate
description: Introduced to Japan from the Asian mainland after the Man'yōshū era. Valued for its brilliant orange blossoms, ornamental fruit, and use in bonsai.

name: Heavenly Bamboo
description: Despite its name, not a true bamboo. Long planted near Japanese entryways for its red winter berries and the auspicious sound of its name (nan-ten, 'turning misfortune').

name: Coast Redwood
description: A California native used here as a tall evergreen backdrop, echoing the role cedar (sugi) plays in Japanese gardens.

name: Indian Hawthorn
description: A compact evergreen shrub with pink-white spring blossoms. A reliable Southern California stand-in for Japanese flowering shrubs.

name: Lilyturf
description: A grass-like groundcover with slender purple flower spikes. Often used in Japanese gardens to soften path edges and stones.

name: Creeping Periwinkle
description: A trailing evergreen groundcover with violet-blue flowers, used here in place of native Japanese groundcovers for its drought tolerance.

name: Juniper 'Old Gold'
description: A spreading juniper with golden-yellow new growth, used as ornamental low cover. A cultivated variety of the broader juniper family found in the Man'yōshū.

name: Golden Rain Tree
description: A small deciduous tree with cascading yellow summer flowers followed by papery lantern-shaped seed pods.

name: Victorian Box
description: An Australian evergreen tree with fragrant cream flowers, used as a screening tree in this Los Angeles adaptation of a Japanese garden.

name: Dwarf Sacred Bamboo
description: A compact cultivar of heavenly bamboo, prized for its dense mounding habit and crimson winter foliage. Planted as a low accent at path edges.
